British · Easy · Serves 2

Where the Cumberland coil fry-up centres pepper, this one centres sage: the whole plate smells faintly of a herb garden next to a butcher's shop, which is the county's breakfast in one sentence. The method is the café fry-up's sequence with one adjustment: Lincolnshires are plumper than standard bangers and want 2–3 extra minutes at a lower heat to cook through without splitting. Slow heat, patient turns, and the plate assembles itself around the pan's perfume.

- **Plump sausages, gentle heat:** Lincolnshires' coarse, open texture renders slower than a fine-ground banger. Medium-low from the start, 14–16 minutes total, and they arrive juicy with unsplit skins. - Everything out of the fridge 15 minutes ahead, plates warming at 100 °C — the café method's standing orders. - The sequence is the café fry-up's: sausages first, fried bread in their fat, bacon and mushrooms next, eggs basted last.

Lincolnshire Sausage Fry-Up

Prep: 10 minutes · Cook: 25 minutes · Total: 35 minutes · Serves 2

Ingredients

The plate

  • 4 Lincolnshire sausages (360 g), at room temperature, pricked once each
  • 4 large eggs (220 g)
  • 3 rashers (150 g) back bacon (optional — the full works)
  • 2 thick slices (140 g) white bread, for fried bread
  • 150 g chestnut mushrooms, halved
  • 200 g baked beans, warmed with 5 g butter
  • 1 large tomato (150 g), halved

Fat and seasoning

  • 10 ml / 10 g neutral oil, to start
  • 10 g butter
  • 2 g fine sea salt (light — the sausage seasons)
  • 1 g black pepper

Instructions

  1. **Sausages slow, 14–16 minutes.** Film the pan with the oil over medium-low heat and lay in the sausages. Turn every 3–4 minutes, cooking to an even deep brown on all sides. Checkpoint — deeply browned, skins taut, juices running clear at a nick — and the nick reveals the coarse, sage-flecked interior that is the sausage's whole point. The pan holds a slick of herb-scented rendered fat.
  2. **Fried bread, then bacon and mushrooms, 8 minutes.** Lay the bread into the sausage fat, press flat, fry 90 seconds a side, and hold warm. Add the bacon (if using) for 4 minutes, pressing flat at contact, and the mushrooms for the last 5, browning them in the accumulating sage fat. The tomato halves go cut-face down for the final 2 minutes. Checkpoint — bread golden and grease-drunk; bacon flat and amber; mushrooms browned and glossy; tomato blistered and slumping. Every component has taken on the sage's perfume — the plate is seasoned by the pan, not the salt cellar.
  3. **Eggs basted in the sage fat, 3 minutes.** Clear the pan's centre, add the butter, and crack in the eggs when it foams — basting the herb-scented fat over the whites until set, 2–3 minutes, yolks running. Checkpoint — lace-edged whites, liquid yolks, and the eggs tasting faintly of sage — the plate's signature bite, exactly as the Cumberland's eggs taste of pepper.
  4. **The plate, quiet around the sausage.** Beans contained to one side (warmed with the butter while the eggs ran), sausages centred, bacon and mushroom flanking, tomato at six, fried bread propped, eggs at the crown. Pepper over the eggs; salt held back. Checkpoint — the complete plate at arm's length — and the smell test is the real one: sage rising off the whole arrangement, the county's breakfast identified from the doorway.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Sausages split and leakedHeat too high for the plump coarse grindMedium-low, 14–16 minutes, patient turns
Grey, boiled-looking skinsPan crowded or sausages wetRoom temperature, dry surface, space in the pan
Plate over-saltedSalted components over the sage fatSalt the eggs only; taste everything else first
Eggs tasted of nothingFat poured off, fresh oil usedThe sage fat is the point — leave the slick in for the eggs

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Leftover cooked sausages keep 3 days** and slice cold into the finest sage-and-onion sandwiches; the components reheat on a tray at 180 °C for 10 minutes. Eggs always fresh. - **Variation — the homemade version:** the homemade Lincolnshire sausages master takes this plate to its summit — the fry-up and the sausage from the same kitchen, one overnight apart. - **Variation — the sage-and-onion plate:** swap in the sage-and-onion sausages and lose the plain mushrooms' neutrality — the sweetest, softest version of the plate. - **The county note:** serve with brown sauce and a strong mug of builder's tea, and the Lincolnshire flat has been faithfully rendered from Land's End to John o' Groats.
